intro: Scarlatti begins with a few plain notes in D major, then crowds the keyboard with chords that bite. Marcelle Meyer plays the sonata’s leaps, trills and collisions on the piano.

sections.label: A · D major, leaps and trills
sections.mNote: A small opening phrase grows into crowded chords

sections.label: A · The opening returns
sections.mNote: The repeat jumps from A major back to D

sections.label: B · A bass under new flats
sections.mNote: B♭ unsettles the second half’s opening

sections.label: B · The second half returns
sections.mNote: The D-major ending sends the piano back to A

sections.label: Coda · Running notes settle in D
sections.mNote: The closing figures reach their home key

relations.label: The first half repeats
relations.basis: The sonata has two repeated halves; the first moves from D towards A. The measured pair falls inside that first half and its repeat, marked near 68 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.967, sustained 48.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 65.5 s (cache/form/scarlatti-sonata-k119.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The second half repeats
relations.basis: The second half returns towards D and is repeated near 204 s. These excerpts compare its later phrases, not the first half or a later Classical sonata-form recapitulation. CENS diagonal mean 0.941, sustained 42.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 72 s (cache/form/scarlatti-sonata-k119.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Three notes, then a leap
cues.text: A few plain quavers above a D-major chord. The right hand begins modestly, then reaches further up the keyboard with each phrase. Soon the left hand joins the running notes, and the two hands start chasing one another.
cues.evidence: Scarlatti, Sonata K. 119, edited by Pierre Gouin (Les Éditions Outremontaises, 2013), bars 1–17. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Crowded keyboard chords
cues.text: The clean single lines acquire handfuls of notes. Scarlatti packs dissonances into repeated chords, then sends the hands running again. The collision is written into the harmony; even a perfectly placed chord has teeth.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, first half, especially bars 55–72: repeated chords with added dissonant notes, followed by running figures. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Back to plain D major
cues.text: The first half has closed in A major. Its repeat sends the piano straight back to the little D-major opening, before the leaps and crowded chords start again. Both halves of this sonata have repeat signs.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, first-half repeat after bar 95, returning to bar 1; the second repeat follows bar 207. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A pupil crosses the border
cues.text: In 1729 Maria Bárbara leaves Portugal for Spain, married to the Spanish heir. Scarlatti follows his royal pupil to Seville. He continues as her private music master; in 1733 the court moves back to Madrid.
cues.evidence: Cristina Fernandes, Scarlatti, Giuseppe Domenico, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 91 (2018): the move to Seville in 1729 and Madrid in 1733. https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giuseppe-domenico-scarlatti_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: A new B♭
cues.text: The second half begins over an A bass, but B♭ arrives in the upper line almost at once. The repeated notes and trills are familiar. The new flats make the floor beneath them less secure.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, bars 96–107: A in the bass, with B♭ in the melody at bar 97 and subsequent chromatic changes. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The second half again
cues.text: A D-major cadence has brought the piano home. The second repeat sends it back to the A bass and the unsettling flats. Scarlatti makes the hands negotiate that crowded route a second time.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, repeat at the end of bar 207, returning to bar 96. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last running notes
cues.text: The closing figures tumble across the keyboard in D major. Trills interrupt the runs, and the hands trade high and low notes before a final descent into the home chord. Scarlatti puts a pause over the last D.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, bars 183–207: running and trilled figures, final D-major cadence and fermata. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A major returns to D
transitions.from: A · D major, leaps and trills
transitions.how: The first half settles on A. The repeat immediately restores the opening D-major chord and its three-quaver melody. After the closing runs and trills, the bare little phrase sounds almost innocent.
transitions.evidence: Gouin edition (2013), bars 91–95 and the return to bars 1–6. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf

transitions.title: B♭ unsettles the A bass
transitions.to: B · A bass under new flats
transitions.how: The A-major close is followed by an A bass at the start of the second half. B♭ enters the right hand in the next bar. The bass stays put while the upper notes turn chromatic; trills and repeated figures carry the phrase onwards.

transitions.title: D major sends us back
transitions.from: B · A bass under new flats
transitions.how: The cadence reaches D major and pauses. The repeat sign then restores the second half’s opening A bass, with its quick B♭ intrusion above. The change of key happens at the restart, without a linking phrase.
transitions.evidence: Gouin edition (2013), final bars 201–207 and return to bars 96–99. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d8/IMSLP295976-PMLP335903-Scarlatti_Sonate_K.119.pdf

transitions.title: The runs find D major
transitions.to: Coda · Running notes settle in D
transitions.how: Repeated-note figures lead into the final D-major runs. The bass alternates D with its dominant, A, while the hands jump between octaves and exchange the quick notes. A last descending run reaches the held D-major ending, marked with a fermata.

composer.epithet: A royal teacher whose sonatas send the hands flying across the keyboard, then bring them together for a song.
facts: Alessandro Scarlatti’s sixth child; born in 1685, the year of Bach and Handel
Maria Bárbara of Portugal, later Queen of Spain; he served her until his death
Naples and Rome; Lisbon from 1719; Spain from 1729
555 in Ralph Kirkpatrick’s catalogue; most survive in manuscript copies
composer.background:
Alessandro Scarlatti had an eagle to launch. Writing to Ferdinando de’ Medici on 30 May 1705, he described his nineteen-year-old son Domenico: “This son is an eagle whose wings have grown; he must not idle in the nest, and I must not prevent his flight.” The boy already had a post as organist at the royal chapel in Naples and operas to his name. His father sent him north towards Venice, by way of Florence, with a recommendation that could hardly be improved upon. Domenico would eventually settle much farther from home, teaching a Portuguese princess whose marriage took them both to Spain.

Born in Naples on 26 October 1685, the same year as J. S. Bach and Handel, Domenico was the sixth of Alessandro’s ten children. His family included singers as well as composers; opera was a family business. He became a salaried royal organist at fifteen. Rome gave him another kind of court: Maria Casimira, the widowed Queen of Poland, maintained a theatre in her Palazzo Zuccari. Scarlatti supplied her with seven operas between 1710 and 1714, working with the poet Carlo Sigismondo Capece and the stage designer Filippo Juvarra. There were words, costumes and human voices in his working life long before it became a matter of sonata numbers.
